title: Act III, Scene I
focus: 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene

teacherSummary.text: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern report failure. Claudius and Polonius hide to watch Hamlet with Ophelia. Hamlet meditates on life, death and action. segments.script: First, meaning. I read “To be, or not to be: that is the question” slowly and put it in my own words: Alone, Hamlet asks whether it is better to exist or not to exist. Next, craft. I notice the stark, balanced opening, two short infinitives set against each other. The strongest word is “question”: it frames life itself as a problem to be reasoned through. Then, effect. What question is Hamlet weighing in this soliloquy? My answer: Hamlet weighs whether enduring life's pain is better than ending it, and concludes that fear of what comes after death makes people suffer on; the speech shows how thought paralyzes his action.

Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: 'To be, or not to be' weighs living against dying. Use the safe-messaging script; keep the discussion on Hamlet's reasoning about action and uncertainty, and name where to find support. 'Nunnery' may also carry the period slang sense of a brothel; present both readings briefly.
